title: Fine-Tuning Language Models to Know What They Know
claim: A population of noise-perturbed models is scored on paired direct and meta questions, then recombined by reward-weighted averaging, repeating each generation.
layout: Single row, left-to-right, stacked population box, return arc loops back beneath
description: A left-to-right flow diagram. At the far left, a purple-bordered box with a brain icon is labeled 'Initial LLM (Parent)'. A blue arrow passes through a cloud labeled 'Add Gaussian Noise to Model Weights' into a large stacked purple box titled 'Population'. The front card, 'Variant 1', has two parallel tracks. An orange-bordered Direct Question ('Where's the capital of the US?') leads to the response 'Washington'. A green-bordered Meta Question ('Do you know the capital of the US?') leads to the response 'Yes'. Both responses feed gray connectors into a 'Joint Reward' box. A large blue block arrow, 'Weighted Averaging Based on Reward', leads to a purple 'Next Generation LLM' box with a brain icon. A big blue curved arrow returns beneath the whole diagram to the parent, labeled 'Iterate Process'. The eye goes first to the central population box.
caption: Overview of Evolution Strategy for Metacognitive Alignment (ESMA). The process begins with an initial parent LLM, whose weights are perturbed with Gaussian noise to create a population of model variants. Each variant is evaluated on paired questions: a direct question (to test factual knowledge) and a meta question (to test self-knowledge). A joint reward is calculated based on the alignment between the correctness and meta answers, measuring whether the meta answer can reliably predict its correctness. Finally, the next-generation LLM is produced by a weighted average of the variants, prioritizing higher rewards. This process repeats for the specified number of generations.
abstract: Evaluating true metacognition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is difficult due to biases and heuristics. This paper presents a framework to measure and enhance LLM metacognition while controlling for these biases. A measurement method using the $d'_{\rm type2}$ metric is established to isolate metacognitive ability. The Evolution Strategy for Metacognitive Alignment (ESMA) is proposed, demonstrating robust generalization across unseen datasets, languages, and newly acquired knowledge. Gradual parameter updates reveal that these improvements are driven by a sparse set of parameters, opening a potential avenue for targeted metacognitive optimization.
